source: NASA history pages, the Apollo 204 Review Board report, NASA safety case studies, UPI archive and NASA technical papers; see each entry. History, not our measurements.
framing: No one has died in a fire in orbit. The fire deaths below happened on the ground, in oxygen-rich air. What was learned from them is why NASA now lights its fires in empty spacecraft.

entries.title: Valentin Bondarenko
entries.where: On the ground, Moscow: a low-pressure test chamber enriched with oxygen
entries.text: A 24-year-old cosmonaut trainee near the end of a long isolation test. A piece of alcohol-soaked cotton landed on a hot plate and the oxygen-rich air let the fire spread fast. He died of his burns hours later, twenty days before Gagarin flew.
entries.changed: His death was kept secret for 25 years and made public in April 1986. It is now remembered as the first warning that oxygen-rich air turns a small flame into a disaster.
entries.note: Some details (the chamber's exact oxygen level, how long he survived) differ between accounts; we give only what they agree on.

entries.title: Apollo 1: Gus Grissom, Ed White, Roger Chaffee
entries.where: On the ground, Launch Pad 34, during a launch rehearsal
entries.text: The cabin held pure oxygen at 16.7 psi. At 6:31 in the evening the crew reported a fire. About fifteen seconds later the cabin ruptured. The review board found no single cause and did not blame any one person.
entries.changed: Flammable materials in the cabin were strictly limited, full-scale fire tests became normal, and a new hatch could be opened in about five seconds.
quote: The Apollo team failed to give adequate attention to certain mundane but equally vital questions of crew safety.
sources: Report of the Apollo 204 Review Board (NASA)
NASA: tribute to the Apollo 1 crew, 2017

entries.title: Apollo 13
entries.where: In flight, on the way to the Moon
entries.text: Wiring damaged during ground testing shorted inside an oxygen tank and set its Teflon insulation burning. The tank burst. The crew of three made it home.
entries.changed: Teflon was removed from the redesigned tanks and the wiring was sheathed in stainless steel.

entries.title: Soyuz 11: Georgy Dobrovolsky, Vladislav Volkov, Viktor Patsayev
entries.where: Returning from the first space station, Salyut 1
entries.text: Not a fire. A valve jolted open as the modules separated before re-entry, and the cabin lost its air. They are the only people to have died above the atmosphere.
entries.changed: Soviet and Russian crews have flown in pressure suits for launch and landing ever since.
sources: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance: 'Descent into the Void'
entries.note: Included because the cabin's air is life support: the same air a fire would poison.

entries.title: Fire on space station Mir
entries.text: An oxygen-generating canister caught fire. The crew put on masks and used three extinguishers while smoke filled the station. Everyone survived. Official reports said about 90 seconds; astronaut Jerry Linenger later said the fire burned for about 14 minutes.
entries.changed: It showed what our site is about: in orbit, smoke does not rise. It goes wherever the air carries it.
quote: I've never seen smoke spread like it did on Mir.

entries.title: Saffire: fires lit on purpose, with no one aboard
entries.where: In orbit, inside empty Cygnus cargo ships after they left the space station
entries.text: NASA started burning large samples in unmanned cargo ships so no crew ever has to learn the hard way. In the last test, Saffire VI, a smoke monitor reached its alarm level at 981 seconds, after much of the hazardous gas had already been released.
entries.changed: This is the data our site is built on.

entries.title: The air the next crews will breathe
entries.text: NASA has studied lower-pressure, oxygen-richer cabin air for exploration, around 8 psi with about a third oxygen. Saffire VI came close, but no large-scale fire test has been run at those conditions yet.
entries.changed: Our ask: pair flame-light sensors with smoke detectors in future fire tests, and test that air before crews breathe it.

dedication: Dedicated to Valentin Bondarenko, Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee, lost to fire in oxygen-rich air, and to every member of the spaceflight family who gave their life to exploration. Ad astra per aspera: a rough road leads to the stars.
